vignette:
He sits in the chair across from me, hands folded, eyes fixed on a spot on the carpet. It takes him a moment to begin, and when he does, his voice is flat, like he is reading a report he no longer believes in. He is thirty-seven, a database administrator for a regional insurance company, and for the past eighteen months his life has been split into before and after.

Before, he says, he was the kind of person who measured certainty in rows and columns. Every query he ran returned predictable results. Every server he maintained followed the same logical rules. He had a wife-now his ex-wife-a small house in the suburbs, and a body that had never given him a reason to worry. He worked with data all day, then came home to cook dinner, mow the lawn, and fall asleep within minutes of putting his head on the pillow.

Then, on a Tuesday afternoon in late November, he started feeling a tightness in his chest. He thought it was heartburn. He drank water, sat at his desk, and tried to focus on a stored procedure that refused to compile. The tightness did not go away. It spread to his jaw. He logged off early, drove himself to an urgent care clinic, and within an hour was being rushed by ambulance to the nearest hospital. He does not remember much of that ride-only the steady beeping of a monitor and a paramedic telling him to stay awake.

The diagnosis was acute myocarditis, a viral inflammation of the heart muscle that nearly caused cardiac arrest. He spent six days in the intensive care unit, two of them sedated and on a ventilator. When he woke, he felt like a piece of machinery that had been torn apart and hastily reassembled. The doctors said he was lucky. They said his heart function would likely recover. They used words like "full prognosis" and "minimal long-term damage."

But his mind did not hear those words the way it used to hear a clean data set. Something broke inside him that has not been restored.

Now, he tells me, he lives in a smaller apartment. His ex-wife left about eight months after he came home. He does not blame her. He stopped being the person she married: silent at dinner, irritable when she touched him, waking up four or five times a night gasping, his hand pressed against his chest. He stopped wanting to see friends, stopped replying to texts, stopped caring about projects he had once enjoyed. At work, he still manages the databases, but he struggles to concentrate. He will stare at a line of code for twenty minutes, reading it over and over, unable to hold the meaning. He double-checks every backup three times because he is afraid of missing something catastrophic.

He avoids hospitals now. He cannot watch any medical drama on television. The sight of a stethoscope makes his jaw tighten. Last month, a coworker mentioned a heart-healthy diet in the break room, and he walked out without eating. He has not had a full physical since his discharge. He tells himself he does not need it, but the truth is, he cannot bear the idea of being examined.

At night, he replays the ambulance ride without wanting to. Sometimes, in his dreams, he is back on the ventilator, awake, unable to move, the tube in his throat. He wakes up with his heart hammering-the very symptom that started it all-and that sends a spiral of panic through him: it is happening again. He checks his pulse obsessively, once, twice, ten times an hour. He has an app on his phone. He owns a home blood pressure cuff. He has memorized the normal ranges for everything.

He knows, intellectually, that the doctors cleared him. He knows the odds of recurrence are low. But no amount of logic fixes the fear that lives in his bones. "I used to trust my body," he says quietly. "Now I feel like I'm running a system that could crash at any second."

He pauses. His eyes do not leave the carpet. He does not say anything else for a long time.
